title: Determine depth map from Stereo pair
aim: To compute a dense disparity map from a rectified stereo pair with block matching and semi-global block matching, and to convert it into a depth map from the geometry of the rig.
objectives: To understand the relation $Z = fB/d$ between depth and disparity for a rectified stereo pair.
To compute disparity maps with StereoBM and StereoSGBM and to see what the block size and disparity range change.
To convert the disparity map into metric depth.
theory: A rectified stereo rig has two cameras a baseline $B$ apart with parallel optical axes. Corresponding points then lie on the same image row, and their column difference $d = x_L - x_R$ is the disparity. Similar triangles give the depth $Z = fB/d$, where $f$ is the focal length in pixels. One pixel of disparity error is about $Z^2/(fB)$ of depth error, so resolution worsens with the square of the distance.
$$Z = \frac{f B}{d}, \qquad d = x_L - x_R, \qquad \Delta Z \approx \frac{Z^2}{f B}\, \Delta d$$

Finding the matching pixel along the row is the correspondence problem. StereoBM compares small windows with the sum of absolute differences and keeps the cheapest disparity: fast, but noisy where the image has no texture. StereoSGBM adds a smoothness penalty, $P_1$ for a one-pixel change and $P_2$ for larger jumps, and minimises the energy by dynamic programming along several image directions, which gives denser, cleaner maps. Failed matches are marked invalid, and a median filter removes isolated errors.
$$E(D) = \sum_{p} C(p, D_p) + \sum_{q \in N_p} P_1 \left[ |D_p - D_q| = 1 \right] + \sum_{q \in N_p} P_2 \left[ |D_p - D_q| > 1 \right]$$
dataset: Middlebury 2006 'Aloe' rectified stereo pair (data/aloeL.jpg and data/aloeR.jpg, 1282 x 1110 px, taken from the OpenCV sample data) processed at half resolution (641 x 555 px).
algorithm: Read the left and right images, resize them to half resolution and convert to grayscale.
Compute the StereoBM disparity (numDisparities 112, blockSize 15) and divide the fixed-point result by 16.
Compute the StereoSGBM disparity (blockSize 5, $P_1 = 600$, $P_2 = 2400$, uniqueness ratio 10, 3-way mode).
Mark disparities $\le 0$ as invalid and apply a $5 \times 5$ median filter.
Repeat SGBM for blockSize 3, 7, 11 and for numDisparities 48, 80, 112.
Convert disparity to depth with $Z = fB/(d + d_{\min})$, $f = 1870$ px, $B = 160$ mm, $d_{\min} = 135$ px.
Plot the pair, both disparity maps, the parameter sweep and the depth map. Save the disparity for experiment 5.

figures.caption: Figure 4.1: Rectified Aloe stereo pair at half resolution. Corresponding points lie on the same row.
Figure 4.2: StereoBM (left) and StereoSGBM (right) disparity maps. White pixels are invalid matches.
Figure 4.3: Effect of blockSize (top) and numDisparities (bottom) on the SGBM disparity map.
Figure 4.4: Depth map from the SGBM disparity with $Z = fB/(d + d_{\min})$, and the histogram of valid disparities.

results: StereoBM returned valid disparities for 61.8 % of the pixels (3.2 to 103.7 px) in about 15 ms. StereoSGBM returned 73.2 % valid pixels (0.7 to 105.4 px) in about 38 ms at $641 \times 555$.

SGBM is smoother on the cloth and the pot. BM leaves holes and wrong patches in the low-texture areas. Small blocks keep the thin leaf tips, and numDisparities must cover the largest true disparity of about 105 px: with 48 the near leaves are lost.
With $f = 1870$ px, $B = 160$ mm and $d_{\min} = 135$ px the depth runs from 1421 mm to 1894 mm (1st to 99th percentile), with a median of 1792 mm.
conclusion: Dense correspondence between the two images of a rectified pair gives a disparity map, and $Z = fB/d$ turns it into depth. Block matching is fast but fails without texture; semi-global matching costs about twice the time and gives a denser, cleaner map that converts directly to metric depth.
